01: Dense, multicultural old-town barri west of La Rambla. It has the MACBA museum and the Rambla del Raval, and is busy day and night.
02: The medieval core of the city around the cathedral and Plaça Sant Jaume, with narrow lanes and Roman remains. Very central, and full of visitors.
03: Former fishermen's quarter on a spit of land between the old port and the beach, with a tight grid of small flats. The sea and seafood restaurants are on the doorstep.
04: Old-town barri around the Santa Maria del Mar church, the Picasso Museum and the Santa Caterina market. Medieval streets, small shops and many bars.
05: Mostly residential barri in the east of the central Eixample, with a local square and market at its centre. Calmer than the streets around the Sagrada Família.
06: The barri around Gaudí's basilica, on the Eixample grid. Crowded with visitors near the church and quiet and residential a few blocks away.
07: The right side of the Eixample, with Modernista landmarks such as Casa Batlló and La Pedrera, upmarket shops and offices. Central, elegant and expensive.
08: Central Eixample west of Carrer de Balmes, with the historic University building and the Hospital Clínic. Known for its restaurants and everyday shops.
09: Mostly residential part of the western Eixample, with wide grid streets, schools and local shops. Calmer than the centre and close to Sants station.
10: Eixample barri around the Sant Antoni market, reopened in 2018 after a long renovation, with a Sunday book and collectables market. Popular with young residents, with many bars.
11: Barri on the slope of Montjuïc, with the Paral·lel theatres and Carrer de Blai, known for its pintxo bars. The parks and museums of Montjuïc are close.
12: Mostly industrial barri between Montjuïc and the Zona Franca, with few homes. A place for logistics and trade rather than for daily life.
13: Large barri on the south-west edge of the city between Montjuïc and the port, with housing blocks and industrial land. Mixed, and still changing.
14: Small, quiet residential barri at the foot of Montjuïc, close to Plaça d'Espanya. Steep streets and little through traffic.
15: Traditional residential barri between Plaça d'Espanya and Sants, with its own market and squares such as Plaça d'Osca. A strong neighbourhood feel.
16: Residential barri on the south side of Sants, near Gran Via and Montjuïc, with low-rise blocks and traditional shops.
17: Mostly residential barri in the west of the Sants district, around Carrer de Badal, with local shops and schools. Quieter than central Sants.
18: Former village around Plaça de Sants, now the centre of its district and home of Barcelona Sants, the city's main railway station. Strong community life and a big August festival.
19: Barri of the Camp Nou, the stadium of FC Barcelona, and of many offices along the Diagonal. Wide streets and a calmer, family feel away from the avenue.
20: Residential barri in the south of Les Corts, built up around the old Maternitat hospital. Calm streets, schools and local shops.
21: Leafy, upmarket barri in the north-west, with villas, the Pedralbes Monastery, the Royal Palace gardens and the university campuses on the Diagonal.
22: Hill barri in the Collserola range, with detached houses, forest and the Tibidabo amusement park. Reached by the Vallvidrera funicular and FGC trains, and car-oriented.
23: Former village that is now a calm upper-city barri, with a real village centre, markets and Plaça de Sarrià. Popular with families.
24: Quiet, upmarket residential barri between Sarrià and Sant Gervasi, with villas and tree-lined streets.
25: Affluent residential barri at the foot of Collserola, with villas, private schools and quiet streets.
26: Upmarket, central barri known for Carrer de Santaló and the Galvany market, with good shops and restaurants close to the Diagonal.
27: Hilly residential barri between Sant Gervasi and Vallcarca, with steep streets, the Turó del Putxet park and views over the city.
28: Hillside barri between Gràcia and Collserola, close to Park Güell, with steep streets and a mix of old houses, new blocks and community projects.
29: Quiet hillside barri on the slopes below Collserola, with steep streets, small squares and a village feel.
30: Small, quiet hillside barri in the Gràcia district, home to Park Güell, with steep streets and a village feel.
31: Formerly an independent town, now Barcelona's bohemian heart, with small squares such as Plaça del Sol, independent shops, bars and the famous street decorations of its August festival.
32: Dense residential barri on the eastern edge of Gràcia, close to the Sagrada Família, with small shops and many bars. Quieter than the centre of Gràcia.
33: Residential barri on the lower slope of the Guinardó hills, close to the Sant Pau hospital site, with a mix of flats, small shops and green corners.
34: Small hillside barri with steep streets and low-rise housing, mostly residential.
35: Large residential barri on the hills of the Horta-Guinardó district, with the Parc del Guinardó and steep streets that make for many stairs and ramps.
36: Small, quiet residential barri on a hillside, with steep streets and low-rise housing.
37: Hillside barri known for its steep streets and for the Bunkers del Carmel, a viewpoint with a 360° view over the city.
38: Residential hillside barri in the north of the city, with steep streets and views, on the slopes below Collserola.
39: Small barri at the edge of Collserola, with low-rise housing and quiet streets, far from the city centre.
40: Planned residential estate from the 1960s: housing blocks set in green space, next to Collserola and the Vall d'Hebron hospital.
41: Home of the Vall d'Hebron hospital campus and of sports facilities built for the 1992 Olympics, at the foot of Collserola.
42: Small, quiet barri between Horta and the Vall d'Hebron hospital, with low-rise housing and a village feel.
43: Former village on the hills with a real village centre and the Laberint d'Horta, the oldest preserved garden in the city.
44: Mostly residential barri in the south of Nou Barris, close to Sant Andreu and Horta, with everyday shops and a mix of older and newer blocks.
45: Residential barri of mid-rise blocks in the south of Nou Barris, with local shops and schools.
46: Hillside residential barri in Nou Barris, with housing blocks from the 1950s and 60s and a strong local community.
47: Small hillside residential barri in Nou Barris, built in the 1950s as workers' housing.
48: Residential barri in Nou Barris with blocks from the 1960s and the Parc de la Guineueta.
49: Hillside residential barri in Nou Barris, on the slope of Collserola, quiet and far from the centre.
50: Hillside residential barri in Nou Barris, with steep streets and a strong neighbourhood identity.
51: Hillside residential barri in Nou Barris, with housing blocks from the 1950s and 60s.
52: Dense residential barri of mid-rise blocks in Nou Barris, built in the 1950s and 60s, with everyday shops and a local market.
53: Residential barri in the north of Nou Barris, next to the ring road, with housing estates from the 1950s and 60s.
54: Hilltop barri at the northern edge of the city, in the foothills of Collserola, with steep streets and views over the Besòs valley.
55: Isolated residential barri at the northern edge of the city, at the foot of Collserola, with dense housing blocks and its own character.
56: Small, quiet barri at the north-eastern end of the city, by the Besòs river, with low-rise housing.
57: Residential barri at the northern edge of the city, by the Besòs river and the Trinitat road junction.
58: Small, quiet barri between the Besòs river and the railway lines, with low-rise social housing.
59: Residential barri beside the Besòs river, first built with low houses for workers in the 1920s and 30s and now being renewed.
60: Former independent town with a village centre around Plaça d'Orfila and Plaça Mercadal, the Fabra i Coats arts centre and a strong local identity.
61: Barri around the Sagrera railway station, one of the city's large urban redevelopment areas, with housing and an industrial past.
62: Quiet residential barri in Sant Andreu, named after the 1952 Eucharistic Congress and the houses built by returnees from the Americas.
63: Mostly residential barri in the south of Sant Andreu, close to the Sagrera, with everyday shops and a lively street life.
64: Dense residential barri east of the Sagrada Família, with everyday shops and a local market.
65: Traditional barri with an industrial past, with the Parc del Clot built on former railway workshops and good train and metro links.
66: Residential barri in Poblenou, with a mix of old low-rise housing and new buildings of the 22@ innovation district.
67: Barri built for the 1992 Olympic Games, with the Olympic Port, the beach, two high towers and a flat grid of streets.
68: Former industrial district that has become a creative and tech hub (22@), with the Rambla del Poblenou, the beaches and converted factories.
69: Newer barri on the north-eastern seafront, around the Diagonal Mar park and shopping centre and the Mar Bella beaches.
70: Working-class residential barri at the north-eastern end of the city, by the Besòs river and the Fòrum seafront.
71: Mostly residential barri in Sant Martí, with mid-rise blocks, close to Poblenou.
72: Former village that is now a dense residential barri, the historic core of the Sant Martí district.
73: Large residential barri in the north of Sant Martí, built mainly in the 1960s and 70s, with wide avenues and a strong local community.
